form: DSHS Retail Food Establishment Inspection Report (Form EH-06)

sources.label: DSHS Marking Instructions (56-item, 2021) — code section references

code_ref_note: Section numbers are FDA Food Code sections as adopted by the Texas Food Establishment Rules (25 TAC Chapter 228). '§228.x' marks Texas-only provisions.

scoring.bands_note: Illustrative only. Austin publishes a numeric score, not an official color grade.
scoring.fail_note: A score of 69 or below fails, and Austin Public Health follows up with a re-inspection.

core.label: Core
core.correct_within: Fix within 90 days or by the next inspection

areas.name: Paperwork & Management
areas.blurb: Start at the office: permit, certificates, records, and who's in charge.

areas.name: Staff & Handwashing
areas.blurb: Watch your team for a few minutes. Hands, gloves, health, and hygiene.

areas.name: Receiving & Storage
areas.blurb: Deliveries, dry storage, and where your food comes from.

areas.name: Coolers & Cold Holding
areas.blurb: Walk-in, reach-ins, and prep rails. Bring a thermometer.

areas.name: Cooking & Hot Holding
areas.blurb: The hot line: cooking, holding, reheating, and cooling.

areas.name: Prep Area
areas.blurb: Cross-contamination, thawing, utensils, and wiping cloths.

areas.name: Dish, Sanitizing & Chemicals
areas.blurb: Dish pit, sanitizer buckets, equipment surfaces, and chemical storage.

areas.name: Facilities & Pests
areas.blurb: Water, plumbing, restrooms, trash, pests, and the building itself.

items.title: Cooling cooked food
items.text: Proper cooling time and temperature
items.plain_language: Cooked food must drop from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F within 6 hours total.
items.check: Find anything cooling right now (soups, rice, braises). Probe it and ask when it came off heat. Is it on track?
items.fix: If it missed the 2-hour mark to 70°F, reheat to 165°F and restart cooling, or throw it out. Going forward, cool in shallow pans or an ice bath and log the times.
items.na_when: You never cool cooked food or room-temperature ingredients that need chilling.

items.title: Cold holding at 41°F
items.text: Proper Cold Holding temperature (41°F / 45°F)
items.plain_language: Cold food that can spoil must stay at 41°F or colder. Inspectors only need to find one item out of temp.
items.check: Probe 2–3 items in every cooler and prep rail. Every one should read 41°F or below. Check the top of the prep rail, which runs warmest.
items.fix: If it's been above 41°F for less than 4 hours, chill it fast (for example in an ice bath). If longer, or you don't know, throw it out. Then fix or service the unit.
items.na_when: You don't hold any food cold.

items.title: Hot holding at 135°F
items.text: Proper Hot Holding temperature (135°F)
items.plain_language: Hot food being held for service must stay at 135°F or hotter.
items.check: Probe everything in steam wells, warmers, and soup kettles. Stir first, then probe the center.
items.fix: If it's been under 135°F for less than 4 hours, reheat to 165°F. If longer, or you don't know, throw it out. Check that the steam table has water and is on high enough.
items.na_when: You don't hold any food hot.

items.title: Cooking temperatures
items.text: Proper cooking time and temperature
items.plain_language: Raw animal foods must reach a safe internal temperature: poultry 165°F, ground meat 155°F, steaks, fish, and eggs for immediate service 145°F.
items.check: Ask your cooks the cooking temperatures for your menu, then probe something coming off the grill or out of the oven.
items.fix: Put the cooking temps on a card at each station and make probing a habit. Re-cook anything that comes up short.
items.na_when: You don't cook any raw meat, poultry, fish, or eggs.

items.title: Reheating for hot holding
items.text: Proper reheating procedure for hot holding (165°F in 2 hours)
items.plain_language: Leftovers or cooked-and-cooled food going back into hot holding must reach 165°F within 2 hours.
items.check: Ask how yesterday's food gets reheated. Is it heated on the stove or in the oven (not the steam table), and checked for 165°F?
items.fix: Reheat on high heat, not in the steam table, and probe for 165°F before it goes into the well. Throw out anything that can't reach 165°F within 2 hours.
items.na_when: You never reheat cooked-and-cooled food for hot holding.

items.title: Time instead of temperature
items.text: Time as a Public Health Control; procedures & records
items.plain_language: If you hold food out of temperature control using time instead (usually 4 hours max), you need written procedures and every pan marked with its discard time.
items.check: Look at any food sitting out at room temperature on purpose. Is it labeled with a discard time, and is that time still in the future?
items.fix: Throw out anything past its time or unmarked. Write a one-page procedure, keep it on site, and label every pan with its discard time when it comes out.
items.na_when: You don't use time instead of temperature to hold food.

items.title: Approved food sources
items.text: Food and ice obtained from approved source; Food in good condition, safe, and unadulterated; parasite destruction
items.plain_language: All food must come from licensed suppliers and be in good condition. No home-made food, no damaged goods, and fish served raw must be parasite-destroyed (frozen).
items.check: Spot-check invoices and storage. Look for food from a home kitchen or retail store with no receipt, swollen or deeply dented cans, or spoiled product.
items.fix: Throw out anything from an unapproved source or in bad condition. Buy only from licensed suppliers and keep invoices. For raw fish, get a parasite-destruction letter from your supplier.

items.title: Receiving temperatures
items.text: Food Received at proper temperature
items.plain_language: Cold deliveries must arrive at 41°F or below, and frozen food must arrive frozen solid.
items.check: Ask whoever receives deliveries whether they probe cold items and reject warm ones. Is there a thermometer at the back door?
items.fix: Probe one or two cold items on every delivery and refuse anything above 41°F or thawed. Put a thermometer where deliveries come in.

items.title: Food separated & protected
items.text: Food Separated & protected, prevented during food preparation, storage, display, and tasting
items.plain_language: Raw meat must never drip onto or touch ready-to-eat food. Food must be covered and protected in storage.
items.check: Open the walk-in. Is raw meat on the bottom shelves (poultry lowest) with ready-to-eat food on top? Are there separate cutting boards for raw and ready-to-eat?
items.fix: Re-stack shelves top to bottom: ready-to-eat, seafood, whole beef or pork, ground meat, poultry. Throw out ready-to-eat food that raw juices touched. Color-code your cutting boards.

items.title: Food-contact surfaces sanitized
items.text: Food contact surfaces and Returnables; Cleaned and Sanitized at ___ ppm/temperature
items.plain_language: Anything that touches food (boards, slicers, knives, prep tables) must be washed, rinsed, and sanitized at the right strength, at least every 4 hours while in use.
items.check: Dip a test strip in the sanitizer buckets and the dish machine or 3-compartment sink. Look closely at the slicer, can opener blade, and ice machine for buildup.
items.fix: Remake sanitizer to the label strength (chlorine is usually 50–100 ppm, quat per the label). Wash, rinse, and sanitize anything dirty right now. Set a 4-hour cleaning schedule for equipment in constant use.

items.title: Returned & unsafe food
items.text: Proper disposition of returned, previously served or reconditioned food
items.plain_language: Food that was served to a customer can't be served again (unopened packaged items excepted), and unsafe food must be thrown out.
items.check: Ask staff what happens to returned plates, unused bread baskets, and salsa. Is anything getting reused?
items.fix: Train staff: once it goes to a table, it goes in the trash. Keep a labeled spot for food set aside to be discarded so it can't get mixed back in.

items.title: Employee health policy
items.text: Management, food employees and conditional employees; knowledge, responsibilities, and reporting
items.plain_language: Your staff must know to report symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice) and certain illnesses to the person in charge, and you need proof they've been told.
items.check: Ask a line cook: "If you had diarrhea, what would you do?" Do you have a signed employee health agreement (such as FDA Form 1-B) for each employee?
items.fix: Have every employee sign an employee health agreement, keep the copies on file, and post a symptom-reporting sign in the kitchen.

items.title: Sick staff kept off the line
items.text: Proper use of restriction and exclusion; No discharge from eyes, nose, and mouth
items.plain_language: Anyone with vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, or certain diagnosed illnesses must be kept from work. Anyone coughing or sneezing a lot or with a runny nose stays away from food.
items.check: Look around: is anyone working who's visibly sick, coughing, sneezing, or wiping their nose?
items.fix: Send sick employees home or move them to a non-food task right away. Make it clear nobody gets punished for calling in sick.

items.title: Handwashing & gloves
items.text: Hands cleaned and properly washed / Gloves used properly
items.plain_language: Staff must wash their hands properly (20 seconds with soap) at the right times, and change gloves between tasks. Gloves don't replace handwashing.
items.check: Watch for 5 minutes. Do people wash hands when they come on the line, after handling raw meat, and after touching their face or phone? Do they wash and put on fresh gloves when they switch tasks?
items.fix: Coach on the spot. Remind staff to wash hands and change gloves between raw and ready-to-eat tasks. Post a "when to wash" sign at every hand sink.

items.title: No bare hands on ready-to-eat food
items.text: No bare hand contact with ready to eat foods or approved alternate method properly followed
items.plain_language: Food that won't be cooked further (salads, garnishes, bread, plated food) can't be touched with bare hands.
items.check: Watch the garnish, salad, and expo stations. Is anyone plating or garnishing with bare hands?
items.fix: Throw out ready-to-eat food that was handled bare-handed. Stock gloves, tongs, and deli paper at every station that handles ready-to-eat food.

items.title: Vulnerable populations
items.text: Pasteurized foods used; prohibited food not offered; Pasteurized eggs used when required
items.plain_language: If you serve a highly susceptible population (daycare, nursing home, hospital), you must use pasteurized eggs and juice and can't serve raw or undercooked animal foods.
items.check: If you serve these groups: are eggs and juice pasteurized? Is anything raw or undercooked on that menu?
items.fix: Switch to pasteurized eggs and juice for these customers and remove raw or undercooked items from their menu.
items.na_when: You don't serve a daycare, nursing home, hospital, or similar vulnerable group.

items.title: Additives & produce washing
items.text: Food additives; approved and properly stored; Washing Fruits & Vegetables
items.plain_language: Only approved additives may be used, and sulfites can't go on fresh produce. Raw fruits and vegetables must be washed before use.
items.check: Do you use curing salts, sulfites, or produce washes? Are they approved and used per the label? Is produce rinsed before cutting?
items.fix: Stop using any unapproved additive. Rinse all produce under running water before cutting or serving.
items.na_when: You don't use any food additives or sulfites on site.

items.title: Chemicals labeled & stored safely
items.text: Toxic substances properly identified, stored and used
items.plain_language: Every chemical must be labeled and stored below and away from food, food equipment, and single-use items.
items.check: Look under and around sinks, prep shelves, and the dish pit. Is there an unlabeled spray bottle, or a chemical stored above or next to food?
items.fix: Label every spray bottle with its contents. Move all chemicals to a dedicated shelf below and away from food. Keep personal medicines and first-aid supplies away from and below food.

items.title: Safe water & backflow
items.text: Water from approved source; Plumbing installed; proper backflow device
items.plain_language: Water and ice must come from an approved supply, and plumbing must stop dirty water from flowing back into it.
items.check: Look at hose bibs (need a vacuum breaker), the mop sink, and drains from the ice machine and prep sinks. They need an air gap, not a hard pipe into the floor drain.
items.fix: Add a vacuum breaker to every threaded faucet with a hose. Have a plumber fix any drain line that connects directly to the sewer.

items.title: Sewage & wastewater
items.text: Approved Sewage/Wastewater Disposal System, proper disposal
items.plain_language: Sewage and wastewater must go into an approved system, with no backups, leaks, or dumping outside.
items.check: Are any floor drains backed up or slow? Any standing water or smell near the grease trap? Is mop water ever dumped outside?
items.fix: Call a plumber for backups now. Get the grease trap pumped on schedule. Dump mop water only in the mop sink.

items.title: Person in charge & food manager
items.text: Person in charge present, demonstration of knowledge, and perform duties / Certified Food Manager (CFM)
items.plain_language: A person in charge who can answer food safety questions must be on site whenever you're open, and so must a Certified Food Manager.
items.check: Who's in charge right now? Could they explain cold-holding temps and when to exclude a sick worker? Is the CFM certificate posted and current?
items.fix: Designate a person in charge for every shift. Get at least one manager certified (an online course plus a proctored exam), and post the certificate.

items.title: Food handler cards
items.text: Food Handler / no unauthorized persons / personnel
items.plain_language: Every food employee needs an accredited food handler certificate within 30 days of hire, and non-staff stay out of the kitchen.
items.check: Pull your employee list. Does everyone who handles food have a current food handler card on file? Are friends, delivery drivers, or vendors wandering through the kitchen?
items.fix: Have anyone missing a card take an accredited online course (about an hour, a few dollars) this week. Keep copies in a binder.

items.title: Hot & cold water
items.text: Hot and Cold Water available; adequate pressure, safe
items.plain_language: Every sink needs hot and cold running water with good pressure. Hand sinks need at least 100°F.
items.check: Run the hot water at the hand sinks, dish sink, and prep sinks for 30 seconds. Does it get hot? Is the pressure good?
items.fix: Have the water heater checked if hot water is slow or missing. If you have no hot water at all, stop food prep until it's fixed.

items.title: Required records & labels
items.text: Required records available (shellstock tags; parasite destruction); Packaged Food labeled
items.plain_language: Keep oyster and clam tags for 90 days and parasite-destruction records for raw fish. Food you package to sell must be labeled.
items.check: If you serve shellfish, are the tags filed by date and kept 90 days? If you serve raw fish, is the supplier's parasite letter on file? Are grab-and-go items labeled?
items.fix: Start a shellstock tag binder and file tags by date as each container empties. Request parasite-destruction letters from suppliers. Label packaged items with name, ingredients, and allergens.
items.na_when: You don't serve shellstock or raw fish and don't package food for sale.

items.title: Variances & special processes
items.text: Compliance with Variance, Specialized Process, and HACCP plan; Variance obtained for specialized processing methods; manufacturer instructions
items.plain_language: Special processes (sous vide, curing, smoking for preservation, and vacuum packing that's held longer than 48 hours) need an approved variance or HACCP plan, and you have to follow it.
items.check: Do you vacuum-pack, sous vide, cure, ferment, or smoke-to-preserve anything? If so, is there an approved plan on site, and are its logs filled in?
items.fix: Stop the process until you have an approved variance or HACCP plan. If you have one, keep the logs current every day.
items.na_when: You don't use specialized processes like vacuum packing, sous vide, or curing.

items.title: Consumer advisory
items.text: Posting of Consumer Advisories; raw or under cooked foods (Disclosure/Reminder/Buffet Plate) / Allergen Label
items.plain_language: If you serve anything raw or undercooked (burgers to order, sunny-side eggs, sushi, oysters), the menu needs an asterisk on those items and a printed warning.
items.check: Find every raw or undercooked item on the menu. Is it marked, and does the menu include the "consuming raw or undercooked…" reminder?
items.fix: Add an asterisk to those items and a footnote: "Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness."
items.na_when: Nothing on your menu is served raw or undercooked.

items.title: Cooling methods & equipment
items.text: Proper cooling method used; Equipment Adequate to Maintain Product Temperature
items.plain_language: You must use fast cooling methods (shallow pans, ice baths, ice wands), and your coolers and hot-holding units must be able to keep food at temperature.
items.check: Are big stock pots or deep containers of hot food sitting in the walk-in? Are coolers overloaded or struggling to stay cold?
items.fix: Split hot food into shallow pans (2 inches deep or less), leave them uncovered until cold, and use ice baths. Get a struggling cooler serviced.

items.title: Date marking
items.text: Proper Date Marking and disposition
items.plain_language: Ready-to-eat perishable (TCS) food kept more than 24 hours must be labeled with a date. It must be used or thrown out within 7 days (the day it was made counts as day 1).
items.check: Pull 5 random containers from the walk-in and reach-ins. Does each have a date, and is it within 7 days?
items.fix: Throw out anything unlabeled or older than 7 days. Put a roll of day-dot labels at every station and do a daily cooler sweep.
items.na_when: You never hold ready-to-eat perishable food for more than 24 hours.

items.title: Thermometers & test strips
items.text: Thermometers provided, accurate, and calibrated; Chemical/Thermal test strips
items.plain_language: You need an accurate probe thermometer, a thermometer in every cooler, and test strips for your sanitizer.
items.check: Is there a working probe thermometer on the line? A thermometer in every cooler? Sanitizer test strips that match your sanitizer?
items.fix: Buy a probe thermometer (around $15) and calibrate it in ice water (it should read 32°F). Put a hanging thermometer in each cooler and keep test strips by the sink.

items.title: Permit current & posted
items.text: Food Establishment Permit (Current & Valid)
items.plain_language: Your food permit must be current and posted where customers can see it.
items.check: Find your permit. Is it posted publicly, and has it not expired?
items.fix: Renew online with Austin Public Health if it's expired, and post it near the entrance or register.

items.title: Hand sinks stocked & clear
items.text: Adequate handwashing facilities: Accessible and properly supplied, used
items.plain_language: Every hand sink must have soap, paper towels, a handwashing sign, and nothing blocking it, and it can only be used for handwashing.
items.check: Visit every hand sink. Is it stocked with soap and towels, with a handwashing sign posted? Is anything stored in it or in front of it? Any dishes, ice, or food in the basin?
items.fix: Restock now and clear anything blocking it. Make "hand sink check" part of every opening and mid-shift checklist.

items.title: Surfaces & equipment in good shape
items.text: Food and Non-food Contact surfaces cleanable, properly designed, constructed, and used
items.plain_language: Equipment and surfaces must be smooth, durable, and easy to clean, in good repair, and approved for food service.
items.check: Look for deeply scored cutting boards, cracked containers, duct-tape repairs, foil or cardboard lining shelves, and household (non-commercial) equipment.
items.fix: Resurface or replace worn cutting boards. Toss cracked containers. Remove cardboard and foil shelf liners. Replace makeshift repairs properly.

items.title: Dish machine & 3-compartment sink
items.text: Warewashing Facilities; installed, maintained, used / Service sink or curb cleaning facility provided
items.plain_language: Your dish machine or 3-compartment sink must work and be used correctly (wash, rinse, sanitize), and you need a mop sink.
items.check: Is the dish machine reaching its listed temperature or sanitizer level? Is the 3-compartment sink set up wash, rinse, sanitize, with test strips nearby?
items.fix: Call your chemical or machine vendor to service the dish machine. Post a diagram showing the 3-compartment sink setup.

items.title: No pests
items.text: No Evidence of Insect contamination, rodent/other animals
items.plain_language: There must be no live or dead pests, droppings, or animals (other than service animals) in the building.
items.check: Use a flashlight under equipment, behind the line, in dry storage, and around door frames. Look for roaches, droppings, gnawed bags, and gaps under doors.
items.fix: Call your pest control company and keep their service reports on file. Add door sweeps, seal gaps, and deep-clean under equipment.

items.title: Personal hygiene
items.text: Personal Cleanliness / eating, drinking or tobacco use
items.plain_language: Staff need hair restraints, clean clothes, and no jewelry beyond a plain band. Drinks need a lid and straw and must be stored away from food, and there's no eating or smoking in prep areas.
items.check: Look at your team: hats or hairnets, clean aprons, no watches or bracelets? Are employee drinks lidded and stored below prep?
items.fix: Keep hats and hairnets at the line entrance. Set up a designated shelf for employee drinks with lids and straws. Remind staff about jewelry.

items.title: Wiping cloths
items.text: Wiping Cloths; properly used and stored
items.plain_language: Wet wiping cloths must be kept in sanitizer between uses, never left on counters or tucked in aprons.
items.check: Are towels sitting on prep counters or hanging from aprons? Are sanitizer buckets set up and at the right strength?
items.fix: Set up a sanitizer bucket at every station and keep cloths in it between uses. Change the solution when it's dirty or tests weak.

items.title: Food protected from contamination
items.text: Environmental contamination
items.plain_language: Food must be protected from drips, dust, splashes, and other contamination, and stored at least 6 inches off the floor.
items.check: Are food boxes on the walk-in floor? Is food uncovered under a dripping condenser? Are ingredient bins open? Are scoops buried handle-down in the product?
items.fix: Get everything onto shelves or dunnage racks. Cover stored food. Fix condenser leaks. Use scoops with handles and store them handle-up.

items.title: Thawing methods
items.text: Approved thawing method
items.plain_language: Thaw food only in the fridge, under cold running water, in the microwave right before cooking, or as part of cooking. Never on the counter.
items.check: Is anything thawing on a counter or in a sink of standing water?
items.fix: Move it to the walk-in or under cold running water. Plan pulls the day before so items thaw in the cooler.
items.na_when: You never thaw frozen food that can spoil.

items.title: Utensil storage & handling
items.text: Utensils, equipment, & linens; properly used, stored, dried, & handled / In-use utensils; properly used
items.plain_language: Clean utensils must be stored clean, dry, and covered or upside down. Utensils in use during service need a proper resting place.
items.check: Are clean pans stacked wet? Are utensils in drawers that are dirty? Are in-use scoops and spoons sitting in water that isn't running or at least 135°F, or with handles buried in food?
items.fix: Air-dry pans before stacking them, upside down. Store in-use utensils in the food with the handle up, on a clean surface, or in a dipper well with running water.

items.title: Single-use items
items.text: Single-service & single-use articles; properly stored and used
items.plain_language: To-go containers, cups, and gloves must be stored off the floor and protected, and single-use items can't be reused.
items.check: Are to-go boxes or cup sleeves on the floor? Are cups stored mouth-up and exposed? Is anyone reusing food buckets or single-use containers?
items.fix: Store single-use items 6 inches off the floor in their sleeves or upside down. Don't reuse single-use containers.

items.title: Bulk containers labeled
items.text: Original container labeling (Bulk Food)
items.plain_language: Food moved out of its original package (flour, sugar, salt, oils, spices) must be labeled with what it is.
items.check: Check bulk bins and squeeze bottles. Is every one labeled with its contents?
items.fix: Label every bin and bottle with the food's common name. Masking tape and a marker work fine.
items.na_when: All your bulk food stays in its original packaging.

items.title: Equipment exteriors clean
items.text: Non-Food Contact surfaces clean
items.plain_language: Parts of equipment that don't touch food (door handles, gaskets, shelves, hood exteriors, fryer sides) must be kept clean.
items.check: Look at cooler gaskets and door handles, shelving, the sides of fryers and ranges, and the inside of reach-in drawers.
items.fix: Add these surfaces to the closing checklist and schedule a weekly deep clean.

items.title: Ventilation, lighting & break areas
items.text: Adequate ventilation and lighting; designated areas used
items.plain_language: Hoods and filters must work and be clean, lights over food need shields, and personal belongings go in a designated area away from food.
items.check: Are hood filters greasy or dripping? Do lights over food areas have shields or covers? Are backpacks and phones on prep tables?
items.fix: Clean or swap hood filters. Replace missing light shields. Set up a hook or locker area for staff belongings.

items.title: Trash & dumpster
items.text: Garbage and Refuse properly disposed; facilities maintained
items.plain_language: Dumpsters and trash cans must be in good repair, kept covered, and emptied often enough, with the area around them clean.
items.check: Go outside. Are dumpster lids closed and the drain plug in? Is there litter or grease around it? Are indoor bins overflowing?
items.fix: Close lids and ask your hauler for a plug or repair. Clean the pad. Empty indoor trash before it overflows.

items.title: Floors, walls & ceilings
items.text: Physical facilities installed, maintained, and clean
items.plain_language: Floors, walls, and ceilings must be smooth, in good repair, and clean, and mops must be hung up to dry.
items.check: Look for missing ceiling tiles, broken floor tiles, grime in corners and under equipment, and mops left standing in buckets.
items.fix: Replace damaged tiles. Deep-clean under and behind equipment. Hang mops on a rack after use.

items.title: Restrooms
items.text: Toilet Facilities; properly constructed, supplied, and clean
items.plain_language: Restrooms must be clean and stocked with toilet paper, soap, and towels, with self-closing doors and a covered bin in women's restrooms.
items.check: Check every restroom: toilet paper, soap, towels, clean surfaces, door that closes on its own, lidded bin in women's room.
items.fix: Restock and clean now. Add restrooms to an hourly or per-shift checklist and fix any door closer that sticks.

items.title: Anything else
items.text: Other Violations
items.plain_language: This is the inspector's catch-all for anything that doesn't fit the other 46 items.
items.check: Do a final lap with fresh eyes. Is anything broken, dirty, or out of place that wasn't covered above?
items.fix: Fix anything you found. If you're unsure whether something counts, call Austin Public Health and ask. They'd rather answer a question than cite you.
